items.painLine: I worry AI will take work and no one's ready.
items.title: More time to live
items.line: When AI saves work, people gain free time and share in the gains.

fixes.title: Trade saved hours for time off
fixes.whatChanges: If AI really saves work, agree to use some of the gain for shorter hours while protecting pay.

fixes.title: Own the tools together
fixes.whatChanges: Build or adopt an AI tool owned and governed by the people who use it.

items.painLine: I see the gap between those with plenty and those struggling grow.
items.title: An affordable home that stays affordable for the next family
items.line: I own my home at a price I can manage, and when I sell, another family gets the same chance.

fixes.title: Buy a home through a community land trust
fixes.whatChanges: The Champlain Housing Trust in Vermont keeps the land and sells only the house, so the price doesn't include the land, and a study found sellers still gained about $12,000 on resale while the home stayed affordable for the next buyer. You build less wealth than in a booming open market, which is the tradeoff.
fixes.example: Champlain Housing Trust · Burlington, VT · 1984 · The trust, in Vermont, keeps the land and sells only the home, so the land cost is not in the price; a Davis and Stokes evaluation found sellers gained about $12,000 on resale while homes stayed affordable; $2.1 million of subsidies retained
fixes.firstStep: Search for a community land trust in your area and check its income limits.

fixes.title: Ask your city to put public land into a land trust
fixes.whatChanges: Cities that own vacant lots or old buildings can hand them to a land trust instead of selling them, so the homes built there stay affordable for good. City council members decide this, usually with little public attention.
fixes.firstStep: Find your city's list of vacant city-owned property, or ask your council member's office for it.

items.painLine: I'm always short on money.
items.title: Borrowing from people I trust while building my credit
items.line: When I need a lump sum, I borrow from a circle of people I know, and my credit score goes up while I repay.

fixes.title: Join a lending circle that reports to the credit bureaus
fixes.whatChanges: In San Francisco, Mission Asset Fund runs lending circles where six to ten people each pay in monthly and take turns receiving the pot, with payments reported to the credit bureaus. In one study, members who started with no credit score or a poor one were almost twice as likely as a comparison group to raise their score by 20 points or more.
fixes.example: Mission Asset Fund lending circles · San Francisco, California · 2013 · Members with no or poor credit almost twice as likely as a comparison group to raise their score 20+ points in 10 months
fixes.firstStep: Look up Mission Asset Fund’s lending circles and check whether they serve your state.

fixes.title: Start a lending circle with friends or coworkers
fixes.whatChanges: Many families already do this informally, under names like tanda, susu or hui. It could let a group set the amount and the order, keep a shared record, and remind everyone when a payment is due.
fixes.example: Mission Asset Fund lending circles · San Francisco, California · 2013 · Members with no or poor credit almost twice as likely as a comparison group to raise their score 20+ points in 10 months
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you’d use this, and think of three people you’d trust to pay in every month.

items.painLine: I'm always short on money.
items.title: Free
items.line: I do not have to work just to get by.

fixes.title: Earn from a skill again and again
fixes.whatChanges: Explore whether a skill could bring in money more than once.

fixes.title: Own a source of income together
fixes.whatChanges: Join or build a business where the people doing the work own a share.

items.painLine: I put things off.
items.title: Letting go of tasks I don’t actually need to do
items.line: I’ve stopped carrying around tasks I was never going to do, and the ones left on my list are ones I mean.

fixes.title: Cross off a task you’ve already decided against
fixes.whatChanges: A task that has sat on the list for months is sometimes one you’ve quietly decided not to do. Crossing it off on purpose frees up the attention it keeps taking every time you see it.
fixes.firstStep: Read your to-do list and cross off one item you’ve kept for months and don’t want to do.

fixes.title: Flip a coin on a decision you’ve put off for months
fixes.whatChanges: In a study published in 2021, the economist Steven Levitt had people who were stuck on a big decision, like quitting a job or a class, let a coin toss guide them. Those the coin told to make the change were happier six months later than those it told to stay put.
fixes.example: Heads or Tails coin-toss experiment (Steven Levitt) · United States (online) · 2021 · People told by a coin to make a change they were stuck on were happier six months later
fixes.firstStep: Write the decision as a yes-or-no question, flip a coin, and notice whether you feel relieved or disappointed.

fixes.title: Pay or trade someone to do a task you dread
fixes.whatChanges: If a task matters but you’ve dreaded it for a year, someone else can often do it for a fee or a trade, like a tax preparer, a handyman, or a friend who enjoys paperwork. Paying for it is a reasonable trade when the dread has been costing you for months.
fixes.firstStep: Write down one task you’d happily pay to never think about again, and look up what it would cost.

items.painLine: I worry AI will take work and no one's ready.
items.title: Hiring software that has to prove it's fair
items.line: When a computer screens my job application, someone has checked that it treats people fairly.

fixes.title: Ask employers whether software screened your application
fixes.whatChanges: Since July 2023, New York City has enforced a law requiring employers that use automated hiring tools to have them audited for bias every year and to tell candidates. You can ask the same question anywhere, even where no law requires an answer.
fixes.example: New York City Local Law 144 on automated hiring tools, and the State Comptroller's enforcement audit · New York City · 2025 · Law passed in 2021 requires employers using automated hiring tools to get a yearly bias audit and notify candidates; enforcement began July 2023; the city found 1 compliance issue among 32 companies, state auditors found at least 17
fixes.firstStep: Next time you apply, email the recruiter and ask whether an automated tool reviews applications.

fixes.title: Ask your city council member to enforce hiring-software rules
fixes.whatChanges: A 2025 audit by the New York State Comptroller found the city had flagged one problem among 32 companies, while the auditors found at least 17. Employers' groups say rules like these add cost, but a law on paper does little without someone checking.
fixes.example: New York City Local Law 144 on automated hiring tools, and the State Comptroller's enforcement audit · New York City · 2025 · Law passed in 2021 requires employers using automated hiring tools to get a yearly bias audit and notify candidates; enforcement began July 2023; the city found 1 compliance issue among 32 companies, state auditors found at least 17
fixes.firstStep: Look up your city council member and send a two-line note asking whether your city regulates AI in hiring.

fixes.title: Write to officials about AI hiring rules
fixes.whatChanges: It could draft a short, specific note to your city council member or state legislator, pointing to New York City's law and the audit of how it's been enforced, for you to edit and send.
fixes.example: New York City Local Law 144 on automated hiring tools, and the State Comptroller's enforcement audit · New York City · 2025 · Law passed in 2021 requires employers using automated hiring tools to get a yearly bias audit and notify candidates; enforcement began July 2023; the city found 1 compliance issue among 32 companies, state auditors found at least 17
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this.

items.painLine: I don't sleep well.
items.title: Evenings free from work messages
items.line: When I finish work, I’m actually finished, and my phone stays quiet until morning.

fixes.title: Agree on quiet hours with your team
fixes.whatChanges: Portugal passed a law in 2021, in effect since 2022: outside working hours, employers aren’t supposed to contact staff except in a real emergency. Your team doesn’t need a law to agree on the same thing.
fixes.example: Portugal Law 83/2021 duty of no contact · Portugal · 2022 · Employers barred from contacting staff in rest periods; breach is a grave violation
fixes.firstStep: Suggest a simple rule, like no work messages between 8pm and 8am, and see who’s in.

fixes.title: Ask lawmakers for a law that protects time off
fixes.whatChanges: Under Portugal’s law, contacting staff during their rest time counts as a serious violation. There’s no data yet on how well the law is enforced or whether people sleep better, but it puts the rule in writing instead of leaving it to how considerate your boss happens to be.
fixes.example: Portugal Law 83/2021 duty of no contact · Portugal · 2022 · Employers barred from contacting staff in rest periods; breach is a grave violation
fixes.firstStep: Send your representative a short note about Portugal’s law and why you’d want one here.

items.line: We can heat our homes and get around without burning coal, oil or gas.

fixes.title: Own clean power together
fixes.whatChanges: Form or join a group that owns a clean power project and agrees who pays and who gains.

fixes.title: Fix homes street by street
fixes.whatChanges: Organize home upgrades together, such as insulation, shade or safer cooling, with fair costs for residents.

items.line: People can stay safe when heat or floods hit, even if they have little money.

fixes.title: Own clean power together

fixes.title: Fix homes street by street
fixes.whatChanges: Organize home upgrades together, such as insulation, shade or safer cooling, with fair costs for residents.

items.painLine: I worry AI will take work and no one's ready.
items.title: AI that helps my coworkers instead of replacing them
items.line: At my company, AI takes over the tedious parts of the work and the people stay.

fixes.title: Suggest a trial with a review before any job cuts
fixes.whatChanges: Klarna leaned heavily on AI for customer service, then started hiring people again in 2025 after its chief executive said the quality had dropped. A trial with a set review date lets a company learn that before it lets anyone go.
fixes.example: Klarna returns to human customer service · Klarna (payments company) · 2025 · CEO said AI customer service gave lower quality; company began hiring human agents again
fixes.firstStep: Suggest to your manager that any AI rollout include a review after three months, with staff input.

fixes.title: Make the case for using AI to train people
fixes.whatChanges: In a 2023 study at one customer support company, newer agents using an AI assistant got 34% more done, and more of the staff stayed on. That was one firm, but it's a real example of AI used to bring people up to speed rather than to cut them.
fixes.example: Generative AI at Work (Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond) · Customer support at one US software firm · 2023 · 5,179 agents; 14% more issues resolved per hour on average, 34% for novice and low-skilled workers; AI assistance also increased employee retention
fixes.firstStep: Share the study's main finding with your manager in two sentences and ask how your team plans to use AI.

items.painLine: I'm not heard by the people in charge.
items.title: Voting in the local elections where a few votes decide
items.line: I vote for mayor, city council and school board, not just for president, because those races are often decided by very few people.

fixes.title: Put the next local election date on your calendar
fixes.whatChanges: A Portland State University study of four cities found mayoral turnout as low as 7% of registered voters, in Charlotte’s primary. When so few people vote, each vote is a much bigger share of the result.
fixes.example: Portland State University 'Who Votes for Mayor' pilot · Portland, Charlotte, Detroit and St. Paul · 2016 · Mayoral turnout as low as 7% (Charlotte primary); registered voters 65+ about 10 times as likely to vote as those 18-34
fixes.firstStep: Look up your city’s next election date on your county elections website and add it to your calendar.

fixes.title: Ask a younger friend to vote with you
fixes.whatChanges: The same study found registered voters 65 and older were about 10 times as likely to vote in those mayoral races as voters 18 to 34. Whoever shows up is who local officials hear from, so a couple of friends who start voting changes who that is.
fixes.example: Portland State University 'Who Votes for Mayor' pilot · Portland, Charlotte, Detroit and St. Paul · 2016 · Mayoral turnout as low as 7% (Charlotte primary); registered voters 65+ about 10 times as likely to vote as those 18-34
fixes.firstStep: Text one friend who usually skips local elections and ask if they want to go vote together.

items.title: Shared ownership
items.line: The people who do the work own a share and have a say in where the gains go.

fixes.title: Own a source of income together
fixes.whatChanges: Join or build a business where the people doing the work own a share.

fixes.title: Put a floor under income
fixes.whatChanges: Create a steady income payment so a loss of paid work need not mean losing the basics.

items.painLine: I'm worried about the planet heating up.
items.title: Eating in a way that is easier on the climate
items.line: I still enjoy what I eat, and my meals put out a lot less carbon than they used to.

fixes.title: Swap beef for chicken, beans or lentils a few nights a week
fixes.whatChanges: A 2018 study of 38,000 farms in 119 countries found that a kilo of beef puts out about 60 kilos of greenhouse gases, while a kilo of peas puts out about one. You don’t have to give up beef to make a big difference; eating less of it does most of the work.
fixes.example: Poore and Nemecek food emissions meta-analysis (via Our World in Data) · 38,000 farms in 119 countries · 2018 · 1 kg of beef emits about 60 kg CO2e versus about 1 kg for peas; transport is under 10% of most foods' emissions
fixes.firstStep: Pick two dinners this week where you'd normally have beef and plan a different protein.

fixes.title: Worry less about where food comes from than what it is
fixes.whatChanges: The same study found that shipping is less than 10% of the emissions for most foods, and about half a percent for beef. Local beef still has a far bigger footprint than imported beans.
fixes.example: Poore and Nemecek food emissions meta-analysis (via Our World in Data) · 38,000 farms in 119 countries · 2018 · 1 kg of beef emits about 60 kg CO2e versus about 1 kg for peas; transport is under 10% of most foods' emissions
fixes.firstStep: Look at your last grocery receipt and circle the three items with meat or dairy in them.

items.painLine: I can't find who's already working on this.
items.title: Seeing who has already raised my issue at city hall
items.line: Before I speak up, I know who has spoken about this at council meetings and what they asked for.

fixes.title: Search past city council meetings for your issue
fixes.whatChanges: Council Data Project, started by a University of Washington professor and a student after they followed a Seattle City Council vote on an arena, turns council meetings in 17 cities into searchable transcripts. People who spoke during public comment are often the ones already organizing, and their names are in the record.
fixes.example: Council Data Project searchable council transcripts · Seattle and 16 other U.S. cities · 2023 · Searchable transcripts and voting records for city council meetings in 17 cities. Started by University of Washington iSchool professor Nic Weber and undergraduate Eva Maxfield Brown after they followed a Seattle City Council vote on a proposed NBA arena
fixes.firstStep: Search your city's meeting minutes or council transcripts for your issue and note who spoke about it.

fixes.title: Look up whether your state lawmakers have taken up the issue
fixes.whatChanges: Open States, a free tool from Plural, shows your state lawmakers from your address and keeps a record of state bills. A bill on your issue usually comes with groups that testified for or against it.
fixes.example: Open States legislator lookup and legislative data · United States · 2026 · Free lookup of your state lawmakers by location, plus bulk legislative data and an API
fixes.firstStep: Enter your address in the Open States lookup and write down your two state lawmakers.

items.painLine: I can't find who's already working on this.
items.title: We can pull it off
items.line: People with different pieces of a shared goal can bring them together and make it happen.

fixes.title: Find the missing piece
fixes.whatChanges: Help a team find who may hold a needed skill, tool, space or source of money, then ask if they want to help.

fixes.title: Share the jobs that recur
fixes.whatChanges: Agree how to split recurring jobs, train backups and let people step back.

items.painLine: I don't sleep well.
items.title: Rested
items.line: I wake up rested and ready.

fixes.title: Find sleep care that fits
fixes.whatChanges: Get help to work out why sleep is hard and what care may fit.

fixes.title: Share the load to protect rest
fixes.whatChanges: Help people agree who covers which duties so each has time to rest.

items.painLine: I don't sleep well.
items.title: A bedroom that stays dark and quiet all night
items.line: Streetlights, early sun and traffic noise stop waking me up.

fixes.title: Put up blackout curtains or wear an eye mask
fixes.whatChanges: A Northwestern study found that one night with a room light on raised people’s heart rate and made their bodies handle sugar worse the next morning. The researchers’ rule of thumb: if you can see things clearly in your bedroom, it’s too bright.
fixes.example: Northwestern Medicine light-during-sleep study · Chicago, IL · 2022 · One night with room light (100 lux) raised heart rate and next-morning insulin resistance vs dim light (3 lux)
fixes.firstStep: Stand in your bedroom tonight with the lights off and notice where light gets in.

fixes.title: Run a steady sound like pink or white noise
fixes.whatChanges: A smooth background sound makes sudden noises like a door or a car less jarring. A 2022 review of 34 studies found the research thin, but pink noise did better than white noise and nobody found it harmful.
fixes.example: Systematic review of white and pink noise for sleep (Capezuti et al.) · Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine · 2022 · 34 studies; 9 of 11 pink-noise studies positive, under a third of white-noise studies
fixes.firstStep: Play a free pink-noise track at low volume tonight and notice whether you wake up less.

fixes.title: Try sleep earbuds that cover up snoring and traffic
fixes.whatChanges: Earbuds made for sleep, such as Ozlo’s, seal out some sound and play quiet masking noise over the rest. They cost about $279, so foam earplugs are worth trying first.
fixes.example: Ozlo Sleepbuds noise-masking earbuds · United States · 2025 · $279; passive seal plus masking sounds, up to 14 hours a charge
fixes.firstStep: Buy a pack of foam earplugs and try them for three nights.

items.painLine: I put things off.
items.title: Understanding the feeling that makes me put things off
items.line: When I notice I’m avoiding something, I can name what it makes me feel and still take the first step.

fixes.title: Name the feeling the task brings up
fixes.whatChanges: The psychologists Sirois and Pychyl argued in 2013 that putting things off is mostly about getting away from a bad feeling right now, like boredom, worry or self-doubt, rather than a lack of willpower. Knowing which feeling you’re dodging often tells you what would make the task easier, such as company for a boring job or a second opinion for a scary one.
fixes.example: Procrastination as short-term mood repair (F. Sirois and T. Pychyl) · 2013 · Review argues procrastination is mainly about escaping bad feelings now, at the cost of the future self
fixes.firstStep: Write the task down, and next to it write the one word for how it makes you feel.

fixes.title: Forgive yourself for the last time you put it off
fixes.whatChanges: In a 2010 study of 134 first-year college students, the ones who forgave themselves for putting off studying for their first exams put off studying less before the next round. Being hard on yourself tends to make the task feel worse, and the students who went easier on themselves did better.
fixes.example: Self-forgiveness and procrastination study (Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett) · Canada · 2010 · 134 first-year students who forgave themselves for procrastinating before first exams procrastinated less before the second
fixes.firstStep: Say or write one sentence letting yourself off the hook for the last delay, then look at what’s next.

items.painLine: I put things off.
items.title: My idea exists
items.line: Something I care about making is real, and I can share it.

fixes.title: Make a small real version
fixes.whatChanges: Choose the smallest version of an idea that someone could use, read or try, then make it.

fixes.title: Change or drop the task
fixes.whatChanges: Talk about changing the task or not doing it if it does not fit.

items.painLine: I'm always short on money.
items.title: Getting every tax credit my family is owed
items.line: When I file my taxes, I get back every credit we qualify for without paying someone to find them.

fixes.title: Check whether you qualify for the earned income tax credit
fixes.whatChanges: The IRS estimates that about one in five people who qualify for this credit don’t claim it. For tax year 2024, families with children could get up to $7,830, and the average credit the year before was $2,743.
fixes.example: IRS estimate of unclaimed EITC · United States · 2025 · About one in five eligible taxpayers miss the credit; up to $7,830 with children for tax year 2024; average $2,743 for 2023
fixes.firstStep: Find last year’s tax return and look for the line labeled earned income credit to see whether you claimed it.

fixes.title: Have your taxes done free at a volunteer tax site
fixes.whatChanges: The IRS supports free tax preparation sites staffed by trained volunteers, mainly for people earning about $70,244 or less. The sites mostly serve people who qualify for the earned income credit, so the volunteers know to look for it.
fixes.example: IRS Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) · United States · 2026 · Free tax preparation by trained volunteers, mainly for people earning about $70,244 or less
fixes.firstStep: Search for the IRS VITA site locator and write down the closest site and its hours.

fixes.title: File past returns to claim credits you missed
fixes.whatChanges: In general, you have three years from a return’s due date to claim a refund, including refundable credits you didn’t know about. Many volunteer sites can prepare past-year returns too.
fixes.firstStep: Make a list of which of the last three years you didn’t file, or filed without claiming any credits.

items.painLine: I see the gap between those with plenty and those struggling grow.
items.title: Getting the tax credits my family is already owed
items.line: Each spring I get back the money the tax system sets aside for working families like mine.

fixes.title: Check whether you qualify for the tax credit for working families
fixes.whatChanges: The IRS estimates that about one in five people who qualify for the Earned Income Tax Credit never claim it, and the average credit was about $2,541 for tax year 2022. The IRS has a free online EITC Assistant that asks a few questions and tells you whether you qualify.
fixes.example: IRS estimate of unclaimed Earned Income Tax Credit · United States · 2024 · About one in five eligible taxpayers don't claim the EITC; average credit about $2,541 (tax year 2022); IRS EITC Assistant checks eligibility
fixes.firstStep: Open the IRS EITC Assistant and answer its questions using last year's income.

fixes.title: Have a trained volunteer do your taxes for free
fixes.whatChanges: The IRS runs free tax preparation sites for people who generally earn about $70,244 or less, and volunteers there know which credits people tend to miss. Most sites are open from January to April, so book early.
fixes.example: IRS Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) and AARP Tax-Aide · United States · 2026 · Free tax preparation for people who generally make about $70,244 or less; locator tool and phone line
fixes.firstStep: Look up the nearest free tax site with the IRS locator tool and write down its hours.

items.painLine: I can't find who's already working on this.
items.title: Knowing which local groups already work on my issue
items.line: When something in my town bothers me, I can name the groups already working on it.

fixes.title: Search nonprofit tax filings for your town and issue
fixes.whatChanges: ProPublica's free Nonprofit Explorer lets you search the full text of the tax forms nonprofits file each year, so a search for your town plus a word like "tenants" or "river" turns up groups whose names never mention it. Small informal groups that never filed won't show up, so treat the results as a starting list.
fixes.example: ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer · United States · 2026 · Free search of nonprofits by name and full text of IRS Form 990 filings, with financial summaries
fixes.firstStep: Search Nonprofit Explorer for your town and one word that describes your issue, and write down the first three groups.

fixes.title: Call or text 211 when the issue is a basic need
fixes.whatChanges: If what you care about is food, housing, rides or health care, 211 is a free, confidential line answered by local specialists, and about 13 million requests reach it each year. The people there know which local groups are actually doing that work.
fixes.example: 211 information and referral line · United States · 2000 · Free, confidential line run by 200+ local organizations; about 13 million requests a year
fixes.firstStep: Dial 211 and ask which groups near you work on the need you care about.

fixes.title: Look at volunteer listings near you
fixes.whatChanges: Groups that need help tend to post it. Idealist, a long-running nonprofit directory, has posted 450,000 volunteer openings over the years, and a search by your ZIP code shows who is active right now.
fixes.example: Idealist nonprofit directory · United States and worldwide · 2026 · More than 200,000 organizations connected with volunteers and job seekers; 450,000 volunteer opportunities posted
fixes.firstStep: Search Idealist for volunteer openings near your ZIP code and note which groups keep showing up.

items.painLine: I can't find who's already working on this.
items.title: Meeting the neighbors who care about the same thing
items.line: I find out that four people on my side of town want the same crosswalk I do.

fixes.title: Say privately what you care about and meet others once enough do
fixes.whatChanges: In Vermont, each new Front Porch Forum stays in a waiting stage until 100 residents sign up, so nobody posts to an empty room. It could work the same way: you say privately what you care about, and only when enough people nearby have said the same would It offer to introduce you, with your permission.
fixes.example: Front Porch Forum neighborhood bulletin boards · Vermont · 2013 · Started in Burlington in 2006; by 2013 open to every Vermont town, with 57,000 members across half the state
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and name the one local issue you would want to meet neighbors about.

fixes.title: Invite neighbors to one meeting about a single issue
fixes.whatChanges: You don't have to wait for a tool. A short note to a neighborhood list naming one issue, one place and one time is how many neighborhood groups began.
fixes.firstStep: Draft a three-sentence invitation naming the issue, a place and a date, and send it to one neighborhood list.

items.painLine: I'm always short on money.
items.title: Comfortable
items.line: I do not have to worry about money often.

fixes.title: Earn from a skill again and again
fixes.whatChanges: Explore whether a skill could bring in money more than once.

fixes.title: Own a source of income together
fixes.whatChanges: Join or build a business where the people doing the work own a share.

items.painLine: I don't sleep well.
items.title: Falling asleep without pills or dread
items.line: I go to bed expecting to sleep, and most nights I do.

fixes.title: Ask your doctor about short, drug-free insomnia therapy
fixes.whatChanges: In a large trial in England’s health service, four short sessions with a practice nurse helped people with insomnia more than the usual advice leaflet, without pills. This therapy isn’t right for everyone, so the nurse checks first.
fixes.example: HABIT trial: nurse-delivered sleep restriction · NHS general practices, England · 2024 · 642 adults; four short nurse sessions cut insomnia scores by 3 points vs leaflet
fixes.firstStep: Write down when you went to bed and got up for the next week, so you have something to bring.

fixes.title: Try an online insomnia course your doctor recommends
fixes.whatChanges: England’s health guidance body recommended an online course called Sleepio over sleeping pills in 2022, after reviewing 12 trials. You do the course on your phone or computer, in your own time.
fixes.example: NICE guidance on Sleepio digital CBT-I · England · 2022 · Recommended over sleeping pills after 12 randomised trials
fixes.firstStep: Ask your doctor at your next visit whether there’s an online insomnia course they’d recommend.

fixes.title: Keep a simple morning sleep diary
fixes.whatChanges: Sleep experts agreed on a standard nine-question morning diary in 2012, and it’s what therapists ask for first. It could ask you those questions each morning and turn the answers into a summary you can show a doctor.
fixes.example: Consensus Sleep Diary (Carney et al.) · Sleep journal · 2012 · A standard 9-question morning diary built by 25 insomnia experts
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you’d use this, and tomorrow morning jot down when you went to bed and when you woke up.

items.painLine: I'm not heard by the people in charge.
items.title: Randomly chosen residents advising on hard questions
items.line: When my state faces a hard question, a group of ordinary residents drawn by lot studies it, and lawmakers have to answer what they recommend.

fixes.title: Learn how a randomly chosen citizens’ assembly works
fixes.whatChanges: In 2016 Ireland drew 99 citizens at random, matched to the census by age, gender, class and region, to study the abortion amendment in its constitution. Most of them, 64%, recommended a change, and in the 2018 referendum 66.4% of voters agreed. People still disagree strongly about the outcome; what drew attention elsewhere was the process.
fixes.example: Irish Citizens' Assembly · Ireland · 2016 · 99 randomly chosen members; 64% backed changing the abortion amendment; the 2018 referendum passed with 66.4%
fixes.firstStep: Read a one-page summary of the Irish assembly and write down one question you’d want such a group in your state to take on.

fixes.title: Ask lawmakers for a permanent citizens’ panel
fixes.whatChanges: Since 2019 the German-speaking region of Belgium has had a 24-person citizens’ council, drawn by lot, that picks topics for citizens’ panels. Their advice isn’t binding, but parliament must debate it twice within a year.
fixes.example: Ostbelgien permanent Citizens' Council · German-speaking Community of Belgium · 2019 · A 24-person council drawn by lot sets topics for citizens' panels; parliament must debate their recommendations twice within a year
fixes.firstStep: Write your state legislator a short note asking whether they’d support a trial citizens’ panel on one local issue.

fixes.title: Ask what lawmakers must do with the panel’s advice
fixes.whatChanges: France’s citizens’ convention on climate made 149 recommendations in 2020. The president rejected 3 outright and the climate bill fully included 46, which left many participants disappointed. A panel works best when everyone knows ahead of time what the government owes it.
fixes.example: French Citizens' Convention for Climate · France · 2020 · 149 recommendations; 3 rejected outright, 46 fully included in the climate bill, others partly included or weakened
fixes.firstStep: In your note, ask what the legislature would be required to do with the panel’s recommendations.

items.painLine: I worry AI will take work and no one's ready.
items.title: Knowing in advance how AI will change my job
items.line: Before a new AI system changes my work, my manager tells us what it will do and asks what we think.

fixes.title: Ask your manager which AI tools are coming and why
fixes.whatChanges: In the European Union, the AI Act requires employers to inform staff and their representatives before using high-risk AI in hiring, promotion or firing. There's no such rule in most of the US, but nothing stops you from asking for the same notice.
fixes.example: European Union AI Act rules for AI at work · European Union · 2024 · Employers must inform staff and representatives before using high-risk AI; workplace emotion recognition prohibited
fixes.firstStep: Bring one question to your next one-on-one: which AI tools is the team planning to use this year?

fixes.title: Agree with coworkers on which tasks you want to keep
fixes.whatChanges: Hollywood writers won a rule in 2023 that AI can't write or rewrite their scripts, though a writer can choose to use it with the studio's consent. A team can talk through the same question informally: which parts of the work you're glad to hand off and which you want to keep doing yourselves.
fixes.example: Writers Guild of America 2023 contract AI terms · Los Angeles and New York · 2023 · AI can't write or rewrite literary material; studios must disclose AI-made materials
fixes.firstStep: Ask two coworkers over lunch which part of the job they'd happily hand to software and which they wouldn't.

items.painLine: I put things off.
items.title: Getting boring tasks done with someone else there
items.line: I sit down with a friend, or on a video call with a stranger, and we both get through the tasks we’ve been avoiding.

fixes.title: Do your task while a friend does theirs
fixes.whatChanges: Having another person nearby, even one doing something completely different, can make it easier to stay with a dull or uncomfortable task. An ADHD coach named this body doubling, and people without ADHD use it too.
fixes.example: Focusmate article on body doubling · 1996 · Body doubling means working with another person present, in person or virtually, while they do something unrelated; term coined by ADHD coach Linda Anderson in 1996; reported benefits strongest among people with ADHD but not limited to them
fixes.firstStep: Text a friend and ask if they’d like to spend an hour this week working on your own lists side by side.

fixes.title: Book a video work session with a stranger
fixes.whatChanges: Focusmate pairs you on video with another person for 25, 50 or 75 minutes: you each say what you’ll work on, work quietly, and check in at the end. Three sessions a week are free.
fixes.example: Focusmate virtual body doubling · Online · Paired 25-, 50- or 75-minute video work sessions; three free sessions a week
fixes.firstStep: Book one 25-minute session for the task you’ve been putting off longest.

fixes.title: Put money on a deadline with a friend as referee
fixes.whatChanges: On stickK, a site started in 2008 by two Yale economists, you set a goal, pick a friend to confirm whether you did it, and put money on it that goes elsewhere if you miss. The co-founder reported that 78% of people who used both money and a referee reached their goal, compared with 35% of those who put no money down.
fixes.example: stickK commitment contracts · New Haven, CT · 2008 · Co-founder reported 78% of users with money and a referee reached goals, versus 35% with no money down
fixes.firstStep: Choose one task, a date, and a friend you’d trust to say honestly whether you did it.

items.painLine: I'm not heard by the people in charge.
items.title: Our money, our say
items.line: People here decide how part of our shared budget is spent.

fixes.title: Let residents decide what gets funded
fixes.whatChanges: Set aside a real public budget and let residents choose which projects it pays for.

fixes.title: Give residents a real vote
fixes.whatChanges: Choose residents from across the community and give them a vote that counts on one public issue.

items.painLine: I'm worried about the planet heating up.
items.title: Knowing which of my choices matter most for the climate
items.line: I put my effort into the few things that make a real dent, and I stop feeling guilty about the rest.

fixes.title: Focus first on driving, flying and food
fixes.whatChanges: A 2017 review of 39 studies by researchers at Lund University found that living without a car saves about 2.4 tonnes of carbon a year, and skipping one round-trip flight across the Atlantic saves about 1.6. Eating plant-based saves about 0.8 tonnes, roughly four times what thorough recycling does.
fixes.example: Wynes and Nicholas review of high-impact personal climate actions · Lund University, Sweden (global literature) · 2017 · Car-free living saves about 2.4 t CO2e a year; each round-trip transatlantic flight avoided 1.6 t; plant-based diet about 0.8 t, roughly 4 times recycling
fixes.firstStep: Write down roughly how many miles you drove and how many flights you took in the past year.

fixes.title: Run your bills through a free household carbon calculator
fixes.whatChanges: The Environmental Protection Agency's calculator asks about your heating, utility bills, cars and recycling, then compares your household with the US average and shows what each change would save. Flights and food aren't included, so add those in your head.
fixes.example: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) household carbon footprint calculator · United States · Free calculator covering home energy, vehicles and waste; gives estimated pounds of CO2 a year against the US average and shows savings from planned actions
fixes.firstStep: Pull up last month's electric and gas bills and enter them in the EPA's carbon footprint calculator.

fixes.title: See your own biggest climate choices ranked in order
fixes.whatChanges: It could ask a few questions about your home, car, flights and meals, then use published averages like the Lund figures to show which two or three changes would cut the most for you in particular.
fixes.example: Wynes and Nicholas review of high-impact personal climate actions · Lund University, Sweden (global literature) · 2017 · Car-free living saves about 2.4 t CO2e a year; each round-trip transatlantic flight avoided 1.6 t; plant-based diet about 0.8 t, roughly 4 times recycling
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and note which of driving, flying, food or home heating you think is biggest for you.

items.painLine: I'm not heard by the people in charge.
items.title: People hold power
items.line: People affected by a public decision have a real way to change it.

fixes.title: Let residents decide what gets funded
fixes.whatChanges: Set aside a real public budget and let residents choose which projects it pays for.

fixes.title: Give residents a real vote
fixes.whatChanges: Choose residents from across the community and give them a vote that counts on one public issue.

items.painLine: I worry AI will take work and no one's ready.
items.title: Tools we control
items.line: We can choose, change or leave the AI tools that shape our work.

fixes.title: Trade saved hours for time off
fixes.whatChanges: If AI really saves work, agree to use some of the gain for shorter hours while protecting pay.

fixes.title: Own the tools together
fixes.whatChanges: Build or adopt an AI tool owned and governed by the people who use it.

items.painLine: I can't find who's already working on this.
items.title: Help that lasts
items.line: Our shared work keeps going without wearing out the same few people.

fixes.title: Find the missing piece
fixes.whatChanges: Help a team find who may hold a needed skill, tool, space or source of money, then ask if they want to help.

fixes.title: Share the jobs that recur
fixes.whatChanges: Agree how to split recurring jobs, train backups and let people step back.

items.painLine: I see the gap between those with plenty and those struggling grow.
items.title: Owning a share of the company I work for
items.line: When the business I work for does well, I get part of the gain, not just my wages.

fixes.title: Ask your boss what happens to the business when they retire
fixes.whatChanges: Project Equity, a nonprofit in Oakland, estimates that baby boomers own 2.34 million American businesses employing 24.7 million people, and one estimate says about 80 percent of those businesses have no plan for what happens next. Selling to the employees is one way to keep the jobs, and the owner still gets paid for the business.
fixes.example: Project Equity estimate of baby boomer–owned businesses · United States · 2017 · Project Equity, an Oakland, California-based nonprofit, says baby boomers own 2.34 million businesses employing 24.7 million people; a separate estimate says 80 percent of these businesses lack a plan for what comes next
fixes.firstStep: Ask your boss, casually, whether they've thought about who takes over when they step back.

fixes.title: Share how one founder handed most of his company to staff
fixes.whatChanges: In 2019 Julian Richer put 60% of Richer Sounds, a UK entertainment retailer with 53 stores, into a trust for its employees, and each of 522 staff got £1,000 for every year they'd worked there, about £8,000 on average. Owners are often more open to this when they hear how another owner did it.
fixes.example: Richer Sounds employee ownership trust · United Kingdom · 2019 · Founder Julian Richer handed a 60% stake in the entertainment retailer, which has 53 stores across the UK, to a trust for staff; 522 employees got £1,000 per year of service, about £8,000 on average
fixes.firstStep: Send the story to one business owner you know who's thinking about stepping back.

items.painLine: I see the gap between those with plenty and those struggling grow.
items.title: A secure floor
items.line: People can count on the basics of life even when paid work dries up.

fixes.title: Own a source of income together
fixes.whatChanges: Join or build a business where the people doing the work own a share.

fixes.title: Put a floor under income
fixes.whatChanges: Create a steady income payment so a loss of paid work need not mean losing the basics.

items.painLine: I'm always short on money.
items.title: Hospital bills cut or forgiven when I can’t pay
items.line: When a hospital bill comes, I find out whether I qualify to have it reduced or erased before I pay anything.

fixes.title: Ask the hospital for its financial assistance application
fixes.whatChanges: Nonprofit hospitals have to offer charity care that reduces or erases bills for patients under an income limit, and each hospital sets its own limit. Asking for the application is how you find out where you stand.
fixes.example: Dollar For charity care help · United States · 2019 · Free nonprofit that files hospital charity care applications; more than $38 million in medical bills cleared since 2019
fixes.firstStep: Search your hospital’s name with the words financial assistance policy, and download the application.

fixes.title: Let a free nonprofit file the application for you
fixes.whatChanges: Dollar For, a nonprofit, prepares charity care applications, sends them to the hospital and follows up, at no cost to patients. The group says it has helped clear more than $38 million in medical bills since 2019.
fixes.example: Dollar For charity care help · United States · 2019 · Free nonprofit that files hospital charity care applications; more than $38 million in medical bills cleared since 2019
fixes.firstStep: Answer the eligibility questions on Dollar For’s website with your household size and income.

fixes.title: Ask for an itemized bill before you pay
fixes.whatChanges: An itemized bill lists every charge, so you can spot duplicates or services you never received. Ask for it before you agree to a payment plan.
fixes.firstStep: Call the billing number on your statement and ask for an itemized bill with the billing codes.

items.painLine: I put things off.
items.title: Choose what to do
items.line: I work on goals I choose.

fixes.title: Make a small real version
fixes.whatChanges: Choose the smallest version of an idea that someone could use, read or try, then make it.

fixes.title: Change or drop the task
fixes.whatChanges: Talk about changing the task or not doing it if it does not fit.

items.painLine: I'm worried about the planet heating up.
items.title: Getting solar power without owning a roof
items.line: Part of the electricity I pay for comes from a solar farm nearby, and my bill is a little lower for it.

fixes.title: Subscribe to a community solar farm
fixes.whatChanges: In Minnesota, community solar gardens reached 939 megawatts in 2024, almost a third of the state’s solar, and subscribers’ bills are expected to drop 3% to 8%. Some people object that bills for non-subscribers rise 2% to 3%, which is why the program nearly ended in 2025.
fixes.example: Minnesota community solar garden program · Minnesota · 2025 · 939 MW in 2024, almost a third of the state's solar; subscribers' bills expected to fall 3% to 8%; repeal dropped in June 2025 after advocates rallied
fixes.firstStep: Search your state name with "community solar" and see whether any program serves your utility.

fixes.title: Ask your state lawmakers to allow plug-in solar panels
fixes.whatChanges: In 2025 Utah became the first state to let people plug solar systems of up to 1,200 watts straight into a home outlet, and the law passed with no votes against. The parts run a few hundred dollars, compared with a $30,000 rooftop quote, but no complete plug-in system had been certified by UL yet when Grist reported on the law.
fixes.example: Utah plug-in solar law (HB 340) · Utah · 2025 · Utah became the first state to allow residents to plug solar systems directly into home outlets; passed with no dissenting votes; output up to 1,200 watts; inverters about $300 and panels $250 to $1,000 versus a $30,000 rooftop quote; in Germany balcony panels added 10% more solar capacity
fixes.firstStep: Look up whether a plug-in solar bill has been filed in your state, and find the names of your two state lawmakers.

fixes.title: Find the community solar programs open to your address
fixes.whatChanges: Community solar rules differ by state and utility, and many people never hear about the programs they could join. It could check your utility and ZIP code and list the open programs, with what each would roughly save you.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and find the name of your electric utility on your last bill.

items.painLine: I don't sleep well.
items.title: Room for rest
items.line: I get enough rest and still have time for the people and things I care about.

fixes.title: Find sleep care that fits
fixes.whatChanges: Get help to work out why sleep is hard and what care may fit.

fixes.title: Share the load to protect rest
fixes.whatChanges: Help people agree who covers which duties so each has time to rest.

items.painLine: I'm not heard by the people in charge.
items.title: Deciding with neighbors how some city money gets spent
items.line: My neighbors and I vote on what gets built in our part of town, and then we see it built.

fixes.title: Vote in participatory budgeting where your city offers it
fixes.whatChanges: In participatory budgeting, residents propose and vote on projects paid for with real public money. In New York City’s 2016–17 round, 102,800 residents voted on how to spend over $40 million across 31 council districts.
fixes.example: New York City Council participatory budgeting · New York City · 2017 · In the 2016-2017 cycle, 102,800 residents voted on how to spend over $40 million in capital funds across 31 council districts
fixes.firstStep: Search your city council’s website for “participatory budgeting” to see if your district takes part.

fixes.title: Ask your council member to let residents decide part of their budget
fixes.whatChanges: In 2009 Alderman Joe Moore of Chicago’s 49th Ward handed residents about $1 million of his ward’s capital money; more than 1,300 people voted, funding beach showers, heated bus shelters and a dog park. Skeptics point out that small organized groups can win more than their share, so turnout matters.
fixes.example: Chicago 49th Ward participatory budgeting · Rogers Park, Chicago · 2009 · Alderman Joe Moore let residents decide about $1 million of ward capital money; over 1,300 voted, funding beach showers, heated bus shelters and a dog park; about 400 people attended nine neighborhood meetings the previous fall, per the May 2012 article
fixes.firstStep: Email your council member’s office and ask whether they’d try participatory budgeting next year.

fixes.title: Get told when your city opens a vote on spending
fixes.whatChanges: It could keep track of which cities and districts run participatory budgeting and let you know when proposals or voting open near you. Cities already publish their schedules, but they’re scattered across council websites.
fixes.example: New York City Council participatory budgeting · New York City · 2017 · In the 2016-2017 cycle, 102,800 residents voted on how to spend over $40 million in capital funds across 31 council districts
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you’d use this.
